reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / IDSA
clinicalPearls: A bloodstream infection attributable to an intravascular catheter, most often a central venous line, in a patient with no other apparent source
Coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, enterococci, Gram-negative bacilli, and Candida species are the usual culprits
Diagnosis is supported by paired blood cultures drawn simultaneously from the catheter and a peripheral vein, with a shorter time to positivity from the catheter (differential time to positivity)
Purulence or erythema at the exit site, or clinical improvement after line removal, supports the diagnosis but is not always present
Management principles centre on removing or exchanging the catheter, particularly for S. aureus, Candida, Pseudomonas, or complicated infection, alongside targeted antibiotics
Antibiotic lock therapy may allow catheter salvage in selected long-term lines infected with less virulent organisms
S. aureus and candidal line infections mandate a search for metastatic complications such as endocarditis, and echocardiography should be considered
Prevention relies on strict insertion and maintenance bundles, hand hygiene, and prompt removal of unnecessary lines
reference.pathophysiology: Intravascular catheters can become infected by several routes: migration of skin flora along the external catheter surface to the tip, contamination of the catheter hub and lumen during handling, haematogenous seeding from a distant focus, or, rarely, contaminated infusate. Microorganisms adhere to the catheter and form a biofilm within a matrix that shields them from host defences and antibiotics, allowing persistent shedding of organisms into the bloodstream. This biofilm explains why eradication frequently requires removing the device rather than antibiotics alone.
additionalDifferentials: Bloodstream infection from another source (urinary, respiratory, abdominal)
Contaminated blood culture from skin flora
Localised exit-site or tunnel infection without bacteraemia
Non-infective causes of fever in a hospitalised patient
infectionMimics: Blood culture contamination with coagulase-negative staphylococci
additionalInvestigations: Paired peripheral and catheter-drawn blood cultures for differential time to positivity
Culture of the catheter tip after removal
Echocardiography when S. aureus, candidal, or persistent bacteraemia is present
Repeat blood cultures to document clearance after starting treatment
Imaging to seek metastatic foci if bacteraemia persists
redFlags: Severe sepsis or septic shock arising from the line infection requiring urgent resuscitation and line removal
Persistent bacteraemia despite appropriate therapy suggesting endocarditis, septic thrombophlebitis, or a retained infected device
S. aureus or Candida bloodstream infection with risk of metastatic seeding
Signs of tunnel or pocket infection or septic thrombosis of the cannulated vein
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the organism and host; uncomplicated coagulase-negative staphylococcal infection often resolves with line removal, whereas S. aureus, Candida, or complicated infections carry higher morbidity, mortality, and risk of metastatic complications.
pitfalls: Continuing to use an infected catheter, especially with S. aureus or Candida, instead of removing it
Misinterpreting a single coagulase-negative staphylococcal culture as contamination or as true infection without corroboration
Failing to seek endocarditis or metastatic foci in S. aureus or candidal bacteraemia
Not confirming clearance of bacteraemia with repeat cultures
management: Remove or exchange the infected catheter, mandatory for Staphylococcus aureus, Candida, Pseudomonas or complicated infection given biofilm-protected organisms
Start empirical broad-spectrum cover with a glycopeptide such as vancomycin plus Gram-negative cover, then de-escalate to targeted therapy on culture and sensitivities
Add an echinocandin antifungal when candidaemia is suspected or confirmed
Antibiotic lock therapy to attempt salvage of selected long-term lines infected with low-virulence organisms
Repeat blood cultures to document clearance and define the duration of therapy
Echocardiography and imaging for endocarditis or metastatic foci in persistent or high-risk bacteraemia
Sepsis supportive care with fluid resuscitation and haemodynamic support as needed
Reinforce insertion and maintenance care bundles and remove unnecessary intravascular devices to prevent recurrence
